rules.rule: Every touch target offers an activation zone of at least 48 × 48dp (approximately 9 mm physical; 48 × 48 px CSS on the web), even if the visible element (24dp icon, XS/S button, checkbox) is smaller: the zone extends beyond the visual.
Pointer targets (mouse, stylus) are at least 44 × 44dp.
Separate adjacent targets by at least 8dp to balance density and precision.
Increased density or component scaling never reduces the interactive target below 48 × 48dp; controls that restore default density retain standard target size.
Text contrast against its background: at least 4.5:1 for regular text, 3:1 for large text (18pt normal or 14pt bold and above).
Meaningful icons, field borders, and grouped button containers achieve 3:1 against the background; an isolated and highly salient element (FAB) is exempt for its container.
Disabled elements are exempt from contrast thresholds, but must remain identifiable as disabled by means other than color alone (disabled attribute, aria-disabled).
Never convey information (error, selection, status) by color alone: add text, icon, shape, or pattern.
Provide standard, medium, and high contrast levels generated by the color system, following the OS contrast setting (prefers-contrast) when available.
Every interactive element reached by keyboard displays a focus ring indicator, visible only for keyboard navigation (focus-visible), 3dp thick offset 2dp outward, in secondary color.
The tab order follows the reading order (DOM order) and visual hierarchy; set initial focus for each screen and components with multiple interactive elements; only one element has focus at a time.
In a composite group (tab bar, navigation bar, list, menu, segmented button group), Tab enters and exits the group, arrow keys move focus inside (roving tabindex).
When a dialog opens, focus goes to its first interactive element and Tab cycles through it; on closing or cancellation, focus returns to the triggering element. A snackbar never traps focus.
On the web, structure each page with ARIA landmarks (header, navigation, main, complementary, footer) and hierarchical headings with a single h1 for the page title, in logical reading order.

Every control has an accessible name: visible text preferably, otherwise label (aria-label) for icon buttons, FAB, and chips without text; a purely decorative icon is hidden from assistive technologies.

Use native elements or ARIA roles matching the behavior (button, link, checkbox, switch, radio, tab, slider, dialog, menu, listbox) and expose their state (checked, selected, expanded, pressed, disabled).
Every function is usable by keyboard (or D-pad), screen reader, switch, and voice; no action requires exclusively a gesture or hover.
Every action reached by gesture (list item swipe, drag) also has visible or accessible access, such as a 'plus' button or menu.
The interface supports text scaling up to at least 200% without loss of content or function: containers that grow in height, consistent horizontal padding, line wrapping rather than truncation.
Prefer single vertical scrolling; do not impose scrolling in two directions at once, including enlarged text.

Support right-to-left languages: mirror layout and directional icons, RTL direction and text alignment; do not invert what maintains fixed orientation (charts, email addresses, media playback, clocks).
If animation reduction is enabled, transitions use short fade or apply without motion, without bounce or parallax.
A snackbar with action does not close automatically; without action, it may disappear after 4–10 s, but information must also appear on the page (label 'Saved' instead of 'Save').
Make the primary action largest and most contrasted; limit simultaneous information quantity; group related elements to reduce cognitive load.
Informative images have alt text describing their function; decorative images have empty alt text.
